Session Details

Part 1 - Reducing Time to Create Integrations Using the Pipeline Concept in SAP Cloud Integration

Date: Tuesday, 3 November 2026 | Time: 09:00–11:00 BST | Level: Beginner to Intermediate

The opening session sets the foundation. We introduce the Pipeline concept, walk through the overall architecture, and explain how the Pipeline reduces integration costs by minimising development and maintenance effort. Expect a clear, step-by-step walkthrough of how the Pipeline processes a message from receipt to delivery so you leave ready for the more hands-on sessions to follow.

What you will learn:

  • The purpose of the Pipeline concept and how it reduces integration development effort
  • The Pipeline architecture and its key building blocks
  • The sequence of Pipeline processing steps, from message receipt to delivery
  • The difference between reusable generic integration flows and scenario-specific flows
  • When the Pipeline approach is the right fit for your use case

Who should attend: Integration Developers, Integration Consultants, Solution Architects, Administrators, Technical Consultants

Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of SAP Cloud Integration and integration flows. Prior experience with SAP Process Integration / Process Orchestration is helpful but not required.

👉Register for Part 1

Part 2 - Understanding the Setup and Operation of the Pipeline Concept in SAP Cloud Integration

Date: Tuesday, 10 November 2026 | Time: 09:00–11:00 BST | Level: Intermediate

With the concept firmly in place, in the second live session we turn to the practical realities of getting the Pipeline up and running. We cover the Partner Directory, the key driver behind the Pipeline and walk through what is involved in implementing the Pipeline for different integration scenarios. The session closes with a close look at message flow, restart, and reprocessing: what happens when a message fails, and how you recover it.

What you will learn:

  • The purpose of the Partner Directory and its role within the Pipeline architecture
  • The setup activities required to implement the Pipeline for an integration scenario
  • The difference between SAP-delivered components and scenario-specific development artefacts
  • How to trace a message through the Pipeline and identify common failure points
  • The available options for restarting and reprocessing failed messages

Who should attend: Integration Developers, Integration Consultants, Administrators, Technical Consultants, Support and Operations Engineers

Prerequisites: Attendance at Part 1 (or equivalent familiarity with the Pipeline concept). Basic knowledge of SAP Cloud Integration, integration flows, and message monitoring.

👉Register for Part 2

Part 3 Migrating from SAP PI/PO to SAP Integration Suite with a Pipeline-Based Approach

Date: Tuesday, 17 November 2026 | Time: 09:00–11:00 BST | Level: Intermediate

In the final session we demonstrate a real migration scenario taking an existing SAP PI/PO interface and moving it to SAP Integration Suite using a Pipeline-based implementation. We then deliver a balanced, honest comparison of Pipeline and non-Pipeline approaches including the benefits, the trade-offs, and the considerations that help you decide which is right for your landscape. The session concludes with an open Q&A across all three weeks' content for your chance to get direct answers from the experts.

What you will learn:

  • How an existing SAP PI/PO interface can be migrated to a Pipeline-based implementation in SAP Integration Suite
  • The key stages of a migration scenario from source interface to deployment
  • A comparison of Pipeline and non-Pipeline implementation approaches and their differences
  • The benefits and trade-offs of each approach
  • How to determine whether the Pipeline concept is appropriate for your specific integration landscape

Who should attend: Integration Developers, Integration Consultants, Solution Architects, Administrators, Technical Consultants

Prerequisites: Attendance at Parts 1 and 2 (or equivalent familiarity with the Pipeline concept and Partner Directory). Basic knowledge of SAP Cloud Integration and integration flows.

👉Register for Part 3

We recommend attending the series in order, as each session builds on the previous one. That said, if you already have solid working knowledge of the Pipeline concept and Partner Directory, you can join at the point that matches your experience level.

We look forward to seeing you in November!

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 2: Content Agent and destinations in Dev
entry.content:
Part 2 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 1 we built CTMS in Central: a service key, a source node, a target node and the route. In this part we move to the Dev subaccount and set up the packer, Content Agent, plus the three connections Integration Suite needs to start a transport.

 

Before you start

In Dev, SAP Integration Suite must be subscribed and the Cloud Integration capability activated. Step 1 fails without it (see "What tripped me up" below).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

This instance lets Content Agent read your integration packages.

  • Create a service instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime with plan api.
  • Give it the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, with grant type client credentials.
  • Create a service key. You need its url, clientid, clientsecret and tokenurl.

Step 2: Content Agent instance and key

  • Create a service instance of Content Agent service with plan standard. This is the packer.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: The three destinations

Go to Connectivity > Destinations in Dev and create three destinations. All three use type HTTP, proxy type Internet and authentication OAuth2ClientCredentials. Type the names exactly as below: Integration Suite looks them up by name.

NameURLClient ID / secretToken Service URL
ContentAssemblyServiceurl from the Content Agent keyuaa clientid / clientsecretuaa url + /oauth/token
CloudIntegrationurl from the Process Integration Runtime key + /api/1.0/transportmodule/Transportclientid / clientsecrettokenurl
TransportManagementServiceuri from the CTMS key (Part 1)uaa clientid / clientsecretuaa url + /oauth/token

Shortcut for TransportManagementService: the Content Agent UI (subscription) can create this destination for you, across subaccounts, from its Cloud Transport Management view. Thanks to  @SvenRullmn  from SAP for this tip in the comments of Part 1. The table above is the manual way, and it is still useful to know which value goes where.

TransportManagementService needs one more thing.

Under Additional Properties, add sourceSystemId with the exact name of the source node from Part 1. This tells CTMS which node the parcel is dropped at.

 

Left: the sourceSystemId property (value blurred). Right: Check Connection on the same destination. Read the message carefully, see below.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • The runtime instance would not create. My first Process Integration Runtime instance in Dev ended in "Creation Failed" with this service broker message: "Service instance could not be created for Process Integration Runtime because the required service/capability is not active for this subaccount. Please subscribe to SAP Integration Suite, and once you've done that, activate required SAP Integration Suite capability, such as Cloud Integration or Graph. Then, try again." The instance is only a door to a running Cloud Integration, so that capability has to exist first. Once it was active, I created the instance again from the Service Marketplace and it went through.
  • A green Check Connection proves less than it seems. The message says "HTTP request (without authentication) ... succeeded". It only shows the address is reachable. It does not test the client ID or secret. My client ID mismatch in TransportManagementService did not show up here; it showed up when I opened the Content Agent screen, and that screen worked as soon as I fixed the client ID.
  • Leave the extra options alone. I kept "Use mTLS for token retrieval" and "Use Basic credentials for token service" unticked and Token Service URL Type on Dedicated. For BTP services talking to each other with service keys, the defaults are right. Change them only if your security team requires certificates instead of client secrets.

Roles for this part

Only the instance roles from step 1. They belong to the Process Integration Runtime instance, not to any user. The user roles you need to click Transport come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Dev can now pack a parcel and drop it at the source node. In Part 3 we go back to Central and set up the second Content Agent, the one that unpacks the parcel into the target, and finally fill in the target node's destination.

entry.title: End-to-End Principal Propagation for AI Agents with SAP Integration Suite, MCP and SAP Cloud Connect
entry.content:
A few months ago, I shared how to expose SAP Integration Suite iFlows as MCP tools so that AI agents could discover and invoke OData operations.

That PoC worked. But it left one important question unanswered:

When an AI agent calls an enterprise API, whose identity is it actually using?

My previous setup used OAuth 2.0 client_credentials: a good fit for machine-to-machine scenarios, but a technical identity is not the human talking to the agent. If every user's requests are executed under the same technical account, backend permissions and audit trails cannot automatically reflect the individual behind each request.

So I built a second PoC: SAP MCP Principal Propagation Inspector. The goal was to send a real end-user identity from an MCP client through SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector to a non-SAP Node.js backend, and have that backend independently validate the identity and enforce its own authorizations.

The result: real end-to-end Principal Propagation, with the backend reporting VERIFIED. More importantly, it refused to return data the authenticated user was not authorized to access.

get_my_orders  |  HTTP 200  |  Principal Propagation: VERIFIED
mTLS system identity: verified
Propagated user certificate: verified
Backend role: SALES
Authorization: 0 of 4 orders visible

Four orders existed. The agent received zero. Not because the language model chose to hide them, but because the backend prevented the data from entering the agent's context.

1. Architecture: MCP, OAuth and X.509 Principal Propagation

 

The complete path looks like this:

MCP Client (Claude / MCP Inspector)
    |  OAuth 2.0 authorization_code, human user
    v
SAP Integration Suite - MCP Server (Integration Cell)
    |  BTP Destination: OnPremise + PrincipalPropagation
    v
SAP Cloud Connector
    |  1. mTLS with SCC SYSTEM certificate
    |  2. Short-lived X.509 END-USER certificate
    |     forwarded as SSL_CLIENT_CERT
    v
Node.js 22 / TypeScript / Fastify backend
    |  Verify system TLS peer BEFORE parsing user header
    |  Validate user certificate and map to principal
    |  Apply local application permissions
    v
Business API response: only authorized data

The key distinction is that two different identities must be verified:

Check Question Evidence Enforcement

SystemWhich machine is connecting?SCC system certificate presented on the TLS socketmTLS verification and peer identity pinning
End userOn whose behalf is it acting?Propagated short-lived X.509 certificateCertificate validation and backend RBAC

A certificate placed in an HTTP header is not automatically trustworthy. The backend first authenticates the transport peer. Only then does it inspect the user certificate, which is delivered through the trusted Cloud Connector path.

2. Build a non-SAP backend with authorization that the agent cannot bypass

I implemented a small REST application in Node.js 22, TypeScript and Fastify, deployed with Docker in a Proxmox homelab. SQLite stores the fictional business data; a React/Vite dashboard provides observability.

 

The MCP tool surface is intentionally small and read-only:

HTTP operation OpenAPI operationId Behavior

GET /api/meget_current_userAuthenticated identity, role and trust information
GET /api/ordersget_my_ordersOnly orders accessible to the authenticated user
GET /api/orders/{id}get_order_by_id403 for an unauthorized order; 404 if it does not exist
GET /api/reports/summaryget_sales_summaryManager-only reporting; SALES gets 403

There is no input parameter that allows the agent to choose an arbitrary user's identity. The API gets the principal exclusively from the validated certificate. Application authorization is computed on the server, not requested by the LLM.

Administrative endpoints under /api/observability/* are protected separately and are not exposed as MCP tools.

OpenAPI is the tool contract

The business-facing contract is an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document that defines the four operations, their parameters, descriptions and response types. A shortened illustration:

paths:
  /api/orders:
    get:
      operationId: get_my_orders
      summary: Get orders visible to the authenticated user
      description: Returns only orders authorized for the
        principal derived from the propagated certificate.
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Authorized orders

The description is part of what the agent sees; the actual authorization remains entirely in the backend.

3. Create the MCP Server in SAP Integration Suite

In SAP Integration Suite → Design → Integrations and APIs, I created an MCP Server artifact and selected HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification as its source type.

Setting PoC configuration

ArtifactMCP Server: MCP_PP_Inspector
RuntimeIntegration Cell
Source typeHTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification
API descriptionFour read-only business operations via OpenAPI 3.0.3
AuthenticationOAuth 2.0 / XSUAA
Authorization scopeAPI.invoke

After importing the OpenAPI contract, I verified the tools exposed by the artifact and deployed the MCP Server to the Integration Cell runtime.

Important: verify the tool names shown by Integration Suite after import. In one iteration, the generated names did not match the original OpenAPI operationId values. The names advertised by tools/list are the ones the MCP client must actually invoke.

 

4. OAuth: switch from a technical client to the actual human

My first test used client_credentials. MCP connectivity worked, but Principal Propagation failed:

The token in header 'SAP-Connectivity-Authentication'
does not contain user info and cannot be used
for Principal propagation

That token represented the technical client. There was no human principal to propagate.

For this PoC, the MCP client instead uses OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code to authenticate the real user against SAP XSUAA. The client obtains a user-context access token and uses it when invoking the MCP Server.

 

Developer Hub agent subscription

  1. Publish the MCP Server in a Developer Hub product.
  2. Create a Subscription for Agent for the specific MCP client.
  3. Choose Tenant XSUAA as the authentication provider.
  4. Enter that client's exact OAuth callback / redirect URI at subscription creation time.
  5. Configure the resulting OAuth Client ID and Secret in the MCP client; use the authorization_code flow, not a shared technical bearer token.
  6. Confirm the user receives the scope required by the MCP authorization policy.

In this scenario the MCP policy expects API.invoke. This differs from my previous Northwind iFlow PoC, where a Process Integration Runtime technical token used ESBMessaging.send.

Lesson learned: in my trial environment, editing the callback URL on an existing Developer Hub subscription did not reliably update the underlying XSUAA OAuth client. Creating a new subscription with the correct callback from the beginning was the reliable fix.

5. Configure the BTP Destination for Principal Propagation

I created a BTP Destination for the backend behind Cloud Connector:

Name=MCP_PP_BACKEND
Type=HTTP
URL=http://<virtual-host>:8443
ProxyType=OnPremise
Authentication=PrincipalPropagation
ProxyProtocol=HTTP
CloudConnectorLocationId=PVE

The three properties that matter most are:

  • ProxyType=OnPremise: the request uses SAP Cloud Connector.
  • Authentication=PrincipalPropagation: the request carries a user context that can be propagated downstream.
  • CloudConnectorLocationId=PVE: the request uses the intended Cloud Connector connection.

The Destination uses http:// for the virtual host in this tested setup. This is not the same as the internal hop to the backend: the Cloud Connector mapping explicitly enables TLS to the Node.js server.

 

6. Configure SAP Cloud Connector

I installed SAP Cloud Connector 2.19.1 in a dedicated Debian container, registered it to the BTP subaccount and configured an access-control entry for the non-SAP backend.

 

6.1 Access control and TLS

Property Configuration

Backend typeNon-SAP System
Internal hostpp-inspector.internal
Port8443
Protocol in SCC UIHTTP with Use TLS enabled
Principal typeX.509 Certificate
System Certificate for LogonEnabled
Resource exposureOnly required backend API resources

 

The backend HTTPS listener requires a trusted client certificate during the TLS handshake. A direct request without that certificate does not reach the REST application.

6.2 Two separate certificate roles

The Cloud Connector system certificate authenticates the machine to the backend over mTLS. Separately, Cloud Connector issues a short-lived end-user certificate for Principal Propagation.

I used a dedicated laboratory CA for user propagation and configured this certificate Subject Pattern:

CN=${email},OU=Propagated User,O=PP Inspector Lab,C=ES

In the tested XSUAA JWT context, ${email} resolved successfully. ${mail}, although seen in other Principal Propagation examples, was unavailable and caused certificate generation to fail.

6.3 Synchronize XSUAA trust

In Cloud Connector → subaccount → Cloud to On-Premises → Principal Propagation, I synchronized the identity provider's signing/trust information.

Without it, Cloud Connector rejected the incoming user context:

SSO token validation failed.
Make sure trust is configured correctly
in the cloud connector.

Do not confuse this with BTP Cockpit → Security → Trust Configuration. The BTP subaccount's identity trust and Cloud Connector's token-signature trust are different configuration points.

 

 

7. Backend verification: trust the connection before the header

I intentionally avoided a design that accepts any request containing an SSL_CLIENT_CERT header. Instead, the backend starts with a mutually authenticated HTTPS channel.

  1. TLS layer: require and validate the Cloud Connector client certificate.
  2. System identity: check the exact trusted identity/pin of the TLS peer.
  3. User certificate: only after transport verification, decode the propagated certificate from the trusted path.
  4. PKI checks: validate certificate signatures, trusted issuer, validity, relevant CA constraints and configured purpose policy.
  5. Authorization: map the resulting principal to a backend role and evaluate business permissions.

That order is deliberate. A valid-looking user certificate injected over an untrusted connection is rejected as TRANSPORT_NOT_VERIFIED before the backend even parses the header.

When a reverse proxy is deployed in front of the application, it must remove any client-supplied identity headers and only forward identity information from an authenticated, trusted source. Simply enabling acceptance of underscored headers is not sufficient.

DEMO and REAL_PP: no confusing simulated tests with SAP evidence

Mode Trust source Maximum verdict

DEMOLocal test CA and simulated scenariosSIMULATED
REAL_PPActual Cloud Connector mTLS + propagated user certificateVERIFIED when all checks pass

The real mode refuses to start without the required TLS material, trusted issuer configuration, administrative protection and Cloud Connector identity pin. Local simulation cannot be mislabeled as a real SAP-verified request.

8. Troubleshooting: the problems that took the most time

These are issues encountered during the actual implementation, with the fixes that worked in this laboratory environment.

8.1 OAuth invalid_client despite valid credentials

MCP Inspector initially returned 401 invalid_client / Bad credentials, while the same OAuth client worked using curl. Isolated tests showed that the authorization-code grant was enabled; the Inspector was reusing stored OAuth credentials from a previous session. Clearing the persisted credentials and using the correct subscription resolved the mismatch.

A related observation from this XSUAA environment: HTTP Basic authentication using raw client_id:client_secret worked, while a percent-encoded Basic variant returned invalid_client. This is the behavior observed for the tested client, not a claim about all XSUAA deployments.

8.2 Backend TLS hostname mismatch

SSLHandshakeException: Invalid server certificate
Peer host '192.168.1.35' does not match certificate DNS names
[pp-inspector.internal, localhost]

The backend certificate contained an IP Subject Alternative Name, but this Cloud Connector configuration rejected the connection when targeting the IP. I changed the Internal Host to pp-inspector.internal and resolved that hostname from the Cloud Connector host. Using the DNS name fixed the handshake.

To investigate the failure I also added instrumentation around Node's TLS events (secureConnection and tlsClientError), because a TCP connection alone did not prove a successful handshake.

8.3 Missing Extended Key Usage in propagated certificates

reasonCode: CERT_MISSING_CLIENT_AUTH_EKU

The local test certificates had the TLS client authentication EKU. The propagated certificates from Cloud Connector in this setup had no EKU extension. Under RFC 5280, the absence of EKU does not itself prohibit use for a particular purpose.

Rather than silently weakening validation, I made the exception explicit and tied it to a dedicated CA:

USER_CERT_REQUIRE_CLIENT_AUTH_EKU=false
USER_CERT_CA_DEDICATED=true

The application refuses to start if the first setting is disabled without the second. This design relies on an explicitly dedicated certificate-issuing authority; it should not be copied unchanged into an environment with a shared corporate CA.

8.4 Distinguished Name ordering

Node.js: C=ES, O=PP Inspector Lab, OU=Principal Propagation,
         CN=PP Inspector Lab User CA
OpenSSL: CN=PP Inspector Lab User CA,OU=Principal Propagation,
         O=PP Inspector Lab,C=ES

Plain string comparison fails even though both representations describe the same DN components. The backend canonicalizes the components for the configured issuer comparison. In a production-grade PKI validator, DN parsing and name matching deserve a standards-compliant implementation rather than naive string operations.

8.5 SSL_CLIENT_CERT disappearing at nginx

nginx may discard incoming header names containing underscores. Without the relevant configuration, the application sees CERT_HEADER_MISSING and it looks like a propagation problem.

underscores_in_headers on;

This line addresses parsing; it is not an authorization measure. Any intermediary handling propagated identity must also strip spoofable incoming identity headers and enforce the trusted TLS boundary.

8.6 Issuer allowlist containing commas

Issuer DNs naturally contain commas. My environment parser used a semicolon delimiter for the issuer allowlist. Treating commas as list separators split a valid DN into invalid fragments and rejected all user certificates.

8.7 Developer Hub callback updates

Updating a subscription callback in the Developer Hub UI did not reliably re-provision the redirect URI on the underlying XSUAA OAuth client. Creating a new client subscription with the correct callback proved more reliable than editing an existing one.

9. Real end-to-end results: the agent cannot see unauthorized data

Once the flow was running, a real MCP tool call reached the backend with a verified Cloud Connector transport and an independently validated user certificate.

HTTP status:                 200
Tool:                        get_my_orders
Principal Propagation:       VERIFIED
Transport mTLS:              VERIFIED
End-user X.509 certificate:  VERIFIED
Authenticated role:         SALES
Authorization decision:     0 of 4 orders visible
Certificate lifetime:       70 minutes (observed)

In a separate authorization comparison, I changed the backend role without changing the MCP tool, the client or the API URL:

Role evaluated by backend get_my_orders get_sales_summary

SALESOnly own authorized orders403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT
MANAGERAll orders allowed by manager policy200 OK

Authorization happened in the backend, not inside the prompt. An agent cannot summarize or leak data that it never receives.

 

9.1 Live Demonstration: From an AI Agent Request to Backend Authorization

After getting the entire configuration working, I wanted to verify the most important part of the architecture: what actually happens when an AI agent invokes a business operation using a real user's identity?

The test follows the complete request lifecycle.

Step 1 — The AI agent invokes an MCP tool

I ask the agent to retrieve business orders. The MCP client invokes the corresponding tool exposed by SAP Integration Suite.

No user ID is passed as a tool parameter. The user's identity comes from the authenticated OAuth session.

 

 

Step 2 — The backend verifies Principal Propagation

The request travels through SAP Integration Suite and SAP Cloud Connector, where the authenticated user context is propagated as an X.509 certificate.

The backend independently verifies the Cloud Connector's system identity through mTLS and validates the propagated end-user certificate.

The observability dashboard reports:

  • Principal Propagation: VERIFIED

  • Transport mTLS: VERIFIED

  • End-user certificate: VERIFIED

  • Backend authorization: ENFORCED

Step 3 — The backend decides what the agent is allowed to see

The most interesting part happens after authentication.

A successfully authenticated user is not necessarily authorized to access every business resource.

In the tested scenario, a SALES user receives 403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT when requesting management reports, while a MANAGER is authorized to access them.

The MCP tools, API endpoint and client remain unchanged. The authorization decision belongs entirely to the backend.

I then changed my backend role from SALES to MANAGER and repeated the exact same MCP request.

The authenticated user, OAuth session, MCP tool and SAP configuration remained unchanged. Only the role assignment in the backend was modified.

This time, the backend returned HTTP 200 with the company-wide sales report instead of HTTP 403 ROLE_INSUFFICIENT.

Same user. Same agent. Same MCP tool. Different backend permissions.

 

 

This is the key result of the PoC: the agent can request a business operation, but it cannot bypass the permissions of the authenticated human. Unauthorized data is rejected before it reaches the AI model.

 

What happened when the token expired?

I also tested an authenticated MCP session across a gap of more than eight hours. The client refreshed its OAuth token without another interactive sign-in, and the later tool invocation arrived with a different newly issued user certificate. Both invocations passed real propagation verification.

This demonstrates refresh within the tested session, not indefinite unattended access: eventually an expired or revoked refresh token may require the person to authenticate again.

10. Observability, tests and security review

I built an observability dashboard that distinguishes facts the backend can actually prove from upstream stages it cannot directly observe:

MCP Client                 NOT AVAILABLE (backend view)
SAP MCP Gateway            NOT AVAILABLE (backend view)
SAP Cloud Connector        VERIFIED
Propagated user cert       VERIFIED
Backend authorization      VERIFIED

This is deliberate. The backend cannot independently verify an upstream MCP exchange that was terminated by SAP Integration Suite, so the dashboard does not invent evidence for those earlier steps.

The PoC includes:

  • 108 automated tests using Vitest, with passing lint, typecheck and build.
  • 17/17 smoke tests against the deployed stack.
  • Two validated OpenAPI 3.0.3 specifications.
  • Contract tests checking that documented OpenAPI routes match the actual Fastify route tree in both modes.
  • Independent adversarial security review using OpenAI Codex; reported findings led to additional tests and fixes for transport trust, certificate identity matching, response disclosure and administration protection.

 

11. What this PoC does — and does not — prove

Demonstrated: real end-user identity propagated through an SAP Integration Suite MCP Server and SAP Cloud Connector into a non-SAP REST backend, followed by cryptographic certificate checks and backend-enforced role authorization. Token refresh was observed across a prolonged authenticated session.

Not demonstrated: deployment against S/4HANA/ABAP, production hardening, load testing at scale, or write operations. The environment used SAP BTP Trial and a Proxmox homelab, and the business dataset was fictional.

The backend certificate-chain checker also does not claim to be a complete RFC 5280 implementation. It does not enforce every path-length, name-constraint, certificate-policy or algorithm-policy rule, and it does not perform CRL/OCSP revocation checking. Those are real limits and must be addressed before adopting this pattern as a production security component.

12. Final thoughts

My first MCP PoC answered:

Can AI agents discover and invoke enterprise APIs through SAP Integration Suite?

This second experiment answers a harder question:

Can the backend enforce the permissions of the actual human behind the agent?

In this tested environment, yes. XSUAA authenticated the user, SAP Integration Suite exposed the MCP tools, Cloud Connector propagated the identity, and the backend independently checked the trust boundary before deciding which business data to return.

The most important result was not the successful 200 OK. It was the data that never reached the AI agent.

Related reading: From SAP Integration Suite iFlow to MCP Tools: Exposing OData APIs to AI Agents (my earlier PoC).

Technologies: SAP Integration Suite, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Connector, MCP, XSUAA, OAuth 2.0, X.509, Node.js, Fastify, TypeScript, Proxmox.

entry.title: Part 1: From OData to MCP: Building an MCP Server with SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Hi everyone!

Recently, I’ve been experimenting with MCP on SAP Integration Suite and looking at a practical question:

What does it actually take to make an existing enterprise API consumable by an AI client through MCP?

Rather than building an AI-specific backend, I wanted to start with something we already know well: an existing OData API.

For this experiment, I used the Business Partner (A2X) API from SAP Business Accelerator Hub and exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on SAP Integration Suite’s Integration Cell runtime.

In this first part, we’ll build the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner OData API → SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell → MCP Server → Developer Hub

By the end of this article, we’ll have an MCP capability deployed on Integration Cell, published through Developer Hub, and ready for an MCP client to consume.

The underlying idea is important: we are not replacing the existing OData API or building a special AI backend. We are making an existing enterprise capability available to a new type of consumer through MCP.

In Part 2, we’ll take the next step: connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and see what happens when the user stops thinking about OData endpoints, entities, filters, and query syntax, and simply expresses what they want in natural language.

 

 

Step-by-Step: From Business Partner OData API to MCP

Step 0: What we are building

In Part 1, we are building the provider side of the end-to-end scenario.

We’ll start with the existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, bring it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, expose selected capabilities through an MCP Server running on Integration Cell, and finally publish that MCP Server through Developer Hub.

The flow we’ll build is:

Business Partner (A2X) API
↓ OData
SAP Integration Suite / Integration Cell
↓
MCP Server
↓
Developer Hub / Product / Subscription

By the end of Part 1, the enterprise capability will be ready for an MCP client to consume.

For more background on MCP in SAP Integration Suite, see the SAP Integration Suite MCP Server documentation.

Step 1: Check the prerequisites

Before we start, make sure your SAP Integration Suite environment is ready.

For this scenario, you will need:

  • SAP Integration Suite with API Management activated
  • An active Integration Cell runtime
  • The appropriate Cloud Integration and API Management roles
  • Access to Developer Hub
  • An API that we can expose through MCP

Don't have an SAP BTP environment?

The good news is that you can also experiment with this scenario using an SAP BTP Trial account.

If you don't already have one, follow the SAP Developer tutorial Get an Account on SAP BTP Trial to set up your trial environment.

Once your SAP BTP Trial account is ready, you can continue with the SAP Integration Suite and Integration Cell setup required for this scenario.

The current SAP hands-on MCP Gateway tutorial also uses an SAP BTP Trial account as a prerequisite, so this is a convenient way to reproduce the scenario without requiring an existing productive SAP BTP landscape.

The MCP Server artifact is currently listed as available with Enhanced, Premium, Trial, and Free Tier SAP Integration Suite service plans. See Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

 
This means you don't necessarily need an existing productive SAP Integration Suite landscape to start experimenting with MCP.

Checkpoint

Before continuing, verify that:

✓ SAP Integration Suite is available
✓ API Management is activated
✓ Integration Cell is active
✓ You have access to Developer Hub
✓ You have an API to use for this exercise

Step 2: Find the Business Partner (A2X) API

For this demo, I wanted to start with an existing SAP business API rather than create a backend specifically for MCP.

A convenient place to explore available SAP APIs is SAP Business Accelerator Hub. The catalogue contains thousands of APIs, so it is worth being precise about which one I used for this scenario.

For this tutorial, I used:

Business Partner (A2X)
API identifier: API_BUSINESS_PARTNER

This is important because searching for “Business Partner” in SAP Business Accelerator Hub returns multiple Business Partner-related APIs and resources. To reproduce this scenario, make sure you are working with the Business Partner (A2X) API rather than another Business Partner integration.

Once you have opened the API, take a few minutes to explore its available resources and operations. For this demo, I'm interested in capabilities that support the following progression:

  1. Find Business Partners.
  2. Retrieve more information about a selected Business Partner.
  3. Present that information to the user in a useful way.

At this point, there is nothing MCP-specific about the backend. We're simply identifying the existing business capability that we eventually want our AI client to consume.

Later, when an MCP client consumes this capability, the underlying business information will still come from this existing enterprise API.

Why this matters

We're not designing an API specifically for an AI client. We're taking a business capability that already exists and introducing a new way to consume it.

Step 3: Make the API available as an API artifact on Integration Cell

Now that we have identified the API we want to expose, let's bring it into SAP Integration Suite.

Navigate to:

Integration Suite → Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Edit → Artifacts → Add → API

For details on creating API artifacts, see Create a Reusable API Artifact.

For our scenario, the result looks conceptually like this:

Business Partner API
        │
      OData
        ▼
┌───────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite     │
│                           │
│ API artifact              │
│ Integration Cell runtime  │
└───────────────────────────┘

 

Configure backend authentication

There is one important detail in my setup.

The Business Partner API used as the backend requires an API key. Therefore, the request from the API artifact to the backend also needs to carry the appropriate backend credential.

I configured the API key on the API artifact/policy side so that the MCP consumer does not need to know or provide the backend credential.

This introduces an important distinction that we will see again later:

SAP Integration Suite
     │
     │ Backend authentication / API key
     ▼
Business Partner API
The credential used by the MCP client to access the MCP Server and the credential used by SAP Integration Suite to access the backend API serve different purposes.

Checkpoint

Before adding MCP to the picture, verify that the API artifact can successfully access the backend.

I found this separation very useful while building the demo. If the API layer works independently, any problem introduced afterwards is much easier to isolate.

Step 4: Create the MCP Server

Now we can put the MCP layer in front of the API.

In SAP Integration Suite, navigate to:

Design → Integrations and APIs → Integration Package → Artifacts → Add → MCP Server

Select the appropriate API as the source for the MCP Server.

You can find a complete example in Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

At this point, the architecture starts to look like this:

MCP Client
     │
     │ MCP
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ MCP Server              │
│                         │
│ Integration Cell        │
└────────────┬────────────┘
             │
             │ OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API
 
This is where the existing API capability starts becoming consumable through an AI-oriented interface.

Step 5: Decide what to expose through MCP

This is an important design point.

Rather than asking:

How many API operations can I expose?

I prefer to start with:

What capabilities does my MCP client actually need?

For this demo, we can work backwards from the desired conversation:

"Find business partners..."
           ↓
Need Business Partner search/retrieval

"Tell me more about the first one..."
           ↓
Need additional Business Partner details

This keeps the MCP capabilities closely aligned with the actual user scenario.

The underlying API still provides the business functions. MCP introduces a way for an AI client to discover and invoke the capabilities we choose to expose.

For additional background, see the MCP Server documentation.

Step 6: Review the MCP policy model

Before deploying the MCP Server, let's take a look at the policy model.

This is an important part of the architecture because the MCP Server doesn't simply expose the backend API directly to the AI client. The MCP request is handled through SAP Integration Suite, giving us a managed layer between the MCP consumer and the enterprise service.

For this demo, I kept the default policy model and reviewed the authentication and authorization configuration before deployment.

Conceptually, we now have:

    MCP Client
        │
       MCP
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite    │
│                          │
│ MCP Gateway / Policies   │
│ MCP Server               │
└────────────┬─────────────┘
             │
           OData
             ▼
    Business Partner API

The important point is that the AI client does not connect directly to the Business Partner API. SAP Integration Suite sits between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise capability.

Two authentication contexts

At this stage it is useful to keep the two security contexts separate:

MCP Client 
 │
 │ MCP client authentication
 │
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication / API key
 │
 ▼
Business Partner API
We will come back to the client side of this authentication model in Part 2, when we connect Joule Work Desktop to the capability exposed here.

Step 7: Deploy the MCP Server

Now deploy the MCP Server to the Integration Cell runtime.

The server side of our architecture is now essentially complete:

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ SAP Integration Suite      │
│                            │
│ Integration Cell Runtime   │
│                            │
│      MCP Server            │
└──────────────┬─────────────┘
               │
             OData
               ▼
       Business Partner API

The SAP tutorial Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents also walks through deploying an MCP Server to Integration Cell.

Checkpoint

Before moving on, confirm that the MCP Server has been deployed successfully.

Now we have the runtime capability. The next question is how our MCP client discovers and consumes it.

Step 8: Publish the MCP Server through Developer Hub

How do I access Developer Hub?

Developer Hub is part of the API Management capabilities in SAP Integration Suite. If you haven't activated it yet, enable Developer Hub in your Integration Suite capabilities first.

Once it is activated, open the product switcher in the SAP Integration Suite header and select Developer Hub.

If you're setting this up for the first time, check the required role collections as well. For the complete setup, see Activating Developer Hub.

This was one of the most important discoveries in my own JWD test.

Once the MCP Server was running on Integration Cell, I published it through Developer Hub as part of a product.

The consumption flow becomes:

Integration Suite
      │
 MCP Server
      │
      ▼
Developer Hub
      │
   Product
      │
      ▼
MCP Consumer

In Developer Hub:

  1. Open Admin Center → Manage Content.
  2. Select the Integration Suite business system.
  3. Open the MCP Servers tab.
  4. Select the MCP Server created earlier.
  5. Choose Create Product.
  6. Provide the product name, ID, and description.
  7. Confirm that the correct MCP Server is included.
  8. Publish the product.

For the detailed publishing flow, see Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite.

For me, this step was the bridge between “I have an MCP Server running” and “I have an MCP capability that my client can actually consume.”

Step 9: Subscribe to the product

Once the product is published, subscribe to it through Developer Hub.

The end-to-end consumption flow is:

Publish MCP Server
        ↓
Publish Product
        ↓
Subscribe to Product
        ↓
Retrieve Credentials
        ↓
Configure MCP Client

This sequence turned out to be particularly important in my JWD setup.

At this point, Developer Hub is doing more than simply making the MCP Server visible. The subscription gives us the consumption information needed for the client connection.

For another end-to-end example of this flow, see Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents.

Step 10: Retrieve the client credentials

After subscribing to the product, retrieve the OAuth credentials needed by the MCP consumer.

And this is where I learned something useful.

Lesson learned from my first attempt

Initially, I tried creating credentials manually through a Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

That turned out not to be the path I needed for this scenario.

Once I published the MCP Server through Developer Hub, subscribed to the product, and used the credentials obtained through that consumption flow, the JWD connection worked.

There's also an important point in the current product documentation: the Process Integration Runtime credential approach is described as an anti-pattern, with credentials obtained through Developer Hub strongly recommended instead.

See Invoke an MCP Server Artifact by Obtaining Credentials through Process Integration Runtime.

So my practical takeaway is:

For this scenario, use the Developer Hub publication, subscription, and credential flow for the MCP client rather than starting with a manually created Process Integration Runtime Service Key.

What we have built

At this point, we have completed the provider side of the scenario:

Business Partner API → API artifact → MCP Server → Integration Cell → Developer Hub → Subscription

The existing Business Partner API remains responsible for the underlying business capability. SAP Integration Suite provides the layer through which selected capabilities are exposed via MCP, while Developer Hub provides the consumption path we will use for the MCP client.

But so far, we have only built the provider side.

The more interesting question is what happens when an AI client starts consuming that capability.

Coming next: From MCP to Natural Language

In Part 2, I'll connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client and move away from API terminology entirely.

Instead of thinking about endpoints or query parameters, we'll ask:

“Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.”

Then we'll continue the same conversation:

“Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.”

And finally:

“Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.”

That's where this experiment becomes much more interesting.

entry.title: Part 2: From MCP to Natural Language: SAP Integration Suite and Joule Work Desktop
entry.content:
Hi everyone, and welcome to Part 2!

In Part 1, we started with an existing Business Partner (A2X) OData API, brought it into SAP Integration Suite as an API artifact, exposed selected capabilities through an MCP Server on Integration Cell, and published the result through Developer Hub.

Now comes the part that originally made this experiment interesting to me.

What happens when the user stops thinking about APIs and simply expresses what they want in natural language?

Our complete architecture now looks like this:

Let's connect JWD and try it.

 

 

Step 1: Connect Joule Work Desktop as the MCP client

 
If you haven't completed the MCP Server and Developer Hub setup yet, start with Part 1: From OData to MCP.

Now we can finally connect the client.

For this demo, I used Joule Work Desktop (JWD) as the MCP client and configured the connection using the MCP endpoint and OAuth information obtained through Developer Hub.

Conceptually, we have now completed the entire architecture:

Joule Work Desktop
        │
       MCP
        ▼
SAP Integration Suite
        │
   MCP Server
        │
Integration Cell Runtime
        │
      OData
        ▼
Business Partner API

Once the connector appeared as available in JWD, the configuration was behind us and I was ready to test the complete flow from the user's perspective using natural language.

This is where things become much more interesting.

Step 2: Ask the first natural-language question

Now comes the fun part.

The prompts in this example are intentionally simple.

I'm not trying to demonstrate advanced prompt engineering or prescribe a specific output format. Instead, I want to see how naturally a user can express an intent when the underlying enterprise capability is exposed through MCP.

In a production scenario, prompts could certainly be more explicit about scope, output format, constraints, and expected behaviour. For this experiment, however, I've deliberately kept them conversational.

Instead of testing the integration using API terminology, I ask JWD:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

What's interesting is what I didn't have to specify:

  • an OData endpoint;
  • an entity name;
  • query parameters;
  • filter syntax; or
  • a response structure.

I simply described what I wanted.

That is a very different consumption experience from working directly with an API.

But underneath that simple sentence, we are still using the Business Partner capability that we started with in Part 1.

Step 3: Continue the same conversation

The next test is deliberately not another independent API request.

I simply continue:

Tell me more about the first one, including its address and contact information.

The interesting phrase here is:

“the first one”

From the user's perspective, this is a continuation of the conversation.

There is no need to copy a Business Partner identifier from one result, work out another API operation, and construct another technical request.

The user simply expresses the next intent in the conversation.

Step 4: Move from data retrieval to business intent

Finally, I take it one step further:

Summarize what we know about this business partner in a way that would be useful before a customer call.

The progression now looks like this:

1. Find enterprise data
             │
             ▼
2. Continue conversationally
             │
             ▼
3. Turn the retrieved information
   into a user-oriented response

This is the point where, for me, the scenario becomes more interesting than simply saying “an LLM can call an API.”

We're starting with existing enterprise capabilities and changing how a user can interact with them.

Step 5: What just happened?

 
Let's return to the architecture one more time:

And this brings us back to the main point of the experiment:

The Business Partner API didn't have to become conversational.

It remains an enterprise API.

The MCP Server makes selected capabilities available through MCP, while SAP Integration Suite provides the runtime layer between the MCP consumer and the underlying enterprise service.

You can find more detail about this architecture in the SAP Integration Suite MCP documentation.

What I learned

A few things stood out to me while putting this scenario together.

1. Existing APIs become more valuable, not less

MCP doesn't mean replacing our existing REST or OData APIs.

In this scenario, the Business Partner API remains the underlying business capability. What changes is the way that capability can be exposed and consumed.

That gives our existing API investments another potential class of consumer: AI clients and agents.

2. The user experience changes dramatically

Compare the traditional API consumption process:

Understand the API
        ↓
Understand the data model
        ↓
Construct the request
        ↓
Process the response

with:

Find business partners in Germany and show me their names and cities.

The underlying business capability can remain the same while the consumer experience becomes completely different.

3. MCP authentication and backend authentication are different concerns

 

This became especially clear while building the demo.

On one side, JWD authenticates as an MCP consumer.

On the other side, Integration Suite has to authenticate when invoking the backend Business Partner API.

JWD
 │
 │ MCP authentication
 ▼
SAP Integration Suite
 │
 │ Backend authentication
 ▼
Business Partner API

Keeping these two concerns separate made the architecture, and the troubleshooting, much clearer.

4. Developer Hub was the missing piece for my JWD connection

 

My initial attempt focused too much on creating credentials directly.

The successful path was:

Deploy → Publish through Developer Hub → Subscribe → Retrieve credentials → Connect JWD

Once I followed that consumption model, the pieces came together.

Closing thoughts

For me, this is where MCP starts to get really interesting.

The exciting part isn't that an AI client can execute an HTTP request. It's that we can take business capabilities that already exist, selectively expose them through MCP, and let users interact with those capabilities in terms of intent rather than API implementation.

The Business Partner API remains an API.

What changed is how the capability is discovered, invoked, and experienced by the user.

And that raises an interesting question for integration architects:

As AI clients become another consumer of enterprise capabilities, how should we design, expose, secure, and govern the APIs behind them?

I'd love to hear how others are exploring MCP in their own integration scenarios. If you've tried connecting MCP clients to SAP Integration Suite, or have a different approach to exposing enterprise APIs to AI clients, please share your experience, questions, or lessons learned in the comments below. Let's learn from each other!

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) in SAP Integration Suite
  • Build and Govern MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite
  • Create an MCP Server for Enterprise AI Agents
  • Create a Reusable API Artifact
  • Discover and Publish MCP Servers from SAP Integration Suite
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub
